title: Count the frequency of each element in an array using HashMap (loop through array, for each element increment its count in the map).
shortTitle: Count the Frequency of Each Element in an Array Using HashMap

s1_definition.profdef: Counting frequencies with a HashMap means iterating once over the input and, for each element, using it as a key and storing how many times it has appeared as the value. The standard technique uses the merge or getOrDefault method to increment the count in one line. Because each lookup and update is average constant time, the whole algorithm runs in linear time, O(n), using O(k) extra space where k is the number of distinct elements.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to know how many transactions each merchant received today. The teller goes through the day's slips one by one. For each slip, she finds the merchant's name in a tally sheet and adds one to their running count, or writes them down with a count of one if they are new. At the end, the tally sheet shows exactly how many transactions every merchant got, in a single pass through the slips.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the array once and bump each element's count in a HashMap using merge or getOrDefault.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting frequencies with a HashMap means iterating once over the input and, for each element, using it as a key and storing how many times it has appeared as the value. The standard technique uses the merge or getOrDefault method to increment the count in one line. Because each lookup and update is average constant time, the whole algorithm runs in linear time, O(n), using O(k) extra space where k is the number of distinct elements.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants to know how many transactions each merchant received today. The teller goes through the day's slips one by one. For each slip, she finds the merchant's name in a tally sheet and adds one to their running count, or writes them down with a count of one if they are new. At the end, the tally sheet shows exactly how many transactions every merchant got, in a single pass through the slips.

**One line to remember:** Walk the array once and bump each element's count in a HashMap using merge or getOrDefault.

sections.s2_technical:
The idea is to build a map from element to count in a single loop. For every element you either start its count at one or add one to its existing count.

The cleanest way uses the `merge` method. For example `frequency.merge(merchant, 1, Integer::sum)` means: if merchant is absent, put it with value one; if present, combine the old value and one using sum. This single line handles both the new and existing cases elegantly. An equally common way uses `getOrDefault`, as in `frequency.put(merchant, frequency.getOrDefault(merchant, 0) + 1)` which reads the current count defaulting to zero and writes back one more. Both are average constant time per element.

After building the map, you can read any element's count with `frequency.get(merchant)` or iterate the entries to report everything. To find the most frequent element you scan the entries once comparing values, and to find elements appearing more than once you keep only entries whose value exceeds one.

A senior-level point is that this frequency map is the foundation of many interview problems: finding the first non-repeating element, detecting the majority element, grouping anagrams, and checking if two arrays are permutations of each other all start with a frequency map. The time complexity is linear because each element is processed once and each map operation is average constant time, which is far better than the quadratic approach of counting each element by rescanning the whole array.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a daily stream of card swipes, each tagged with the merchant category code such as GROCERY, FUEL, or DINING. The analytics team needs to know how many swipes happened in each category today to spot spending patterns and possible fraud spikes. We need to count occurrences of each category in one pass. This is exactly a frequency count with a HashMap, where the category is the key and the swipe count is the value.

Problem 2 — Once we have the counts, the fraud team wants the single busiest category, because a sudden surge in one category can indicate card testing. Scanning the frequency map once for the highest count gives that answer cheaply.

In our mini-project we build a `SwipeAnalyzer` with a `countByCategory` method that returns the frequency map, and a `busiestCategory` method that returns the category with the most swipes. The demo feeds a day's worth of category codes and logs the counts and the busiest category.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the swipe array GROCERY, FUEL, GROCERY, DINING, GROCERY, FUEL, DINING, GROCERY.

Step 1: We start with an empty frequency map. We read the first element GROCERY. It is absent, so merge inserts it with count one.

Step 2: We read FUEL. Absent, so merge inserts it with count one. The map now has GROCERY one and FUEL one.

Step 3: We read GROCERY again. It is present with count one, so merge adds one making GROCERY count two.

Step 4: We read DINING, absent, inserted with count one. We read GROCERY a third time, so it becomes count three.

Step 5: We read FUEL again making it count two, then DINING again making it count two, then GROCERY a fourth time making it count four.

Step 6: The loop ends. The final map is GROCERY four, FUEL two, DINING two. We then scan the map once: GROCERY has the highest count, so it is the busiest category.

```
[2026-10-26 19:55:03] INFO    Counted 8 swipes into 3 categories.
[2026-10-26 19:55:03] INFO    GROCERY swipes: 4
[2026-10-26 19:55:03] INFO    FUEL swipes: 2
[2026-10-26 19:55:03] INFO    DINING swipes: 2
[2026-10-26 19:55:03] INFO    Busiest category today: GROCERY
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  swipes[] = [GROCERY, FUEL, GROCERY, DINING, GROCERY, FUEL, DINING, GROCERY]
    │
    ▼ single pass, merge(category, 1, sum)
  GROCERY: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
  FUEL:    1 → 2
  DINING:  1 → 2
    │
    ▼ scan entries for max value
  busiest = GROCERY (count 4)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To count the frequency of each element in an array I use a HashMap where the element is the key and its occurrence count is the value, and I build it in a single pass over the array. For each element I either start its count at one if it is new or add one to its existing count. The cleanest way in Java is the merge method, where I write merge of the key, one, and integer sum, which inserts one if the key is absent and otherwise adds one to the existing count in a single line. The equally common alternative is getOrDefault, reading the current count defaulting to zero and writing back one more.

The reason this is efficient is that each element is processed exactly once and each map operation is average constant time, so the whole thing is linear in the size of the array. That is far better than the naive approach of counting each element by rescanning the entire array, which would be quadratic.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to analyze the daily stream of card swipes tagged by merchant category. In one pass I build a map of category to swipe count, and then I scan that map once to find the busiest category, because a sudden surge in one category can signal card testing fraud. The analytics feed straight into a monitoring dashboard.

The broader point I always make is that a frequency map is a foundational building block. Problems like finding the first non-repeating element, detecting a majority element, grouping anagrams, or checking whether two arrays are permutations of each other all begin with exactly this frequency map. Once an interviewer sees that I reach for a HashMap tally naturally and reason about its linear time complexity, it signals that I can turn a vague counting requirement into an efficient, production-ready solution.
